muga-silk.types: Muga silk comes from Antheraea assamensis reared outdoors on som and other host trees in Assam, and is the rarest of India's commercial silks: the Ministry of Textiles reports roughly 230 tonnes, about 0.6 percent of Indian raw silk, in its 2025-26 annual report. Trade forms are reeled raw muga yarn, spun muga from pierced cocoons and waste, and blends with mulberry (pat) silk or cotton. Assam's silk tradition groups muga with eri and pat. Muga Silk of Assam has been a registered geographical indication since 2007, and a GI logo followed in 2014, with the Assam Science Technology and Environment Council as its registered proprietor.
muga-silk.fabrics: Muga is woven mainly on handlooms around Sualkuchi and other Assamese weaving centers into the mekhela chador (a two-piece garment), riha, saris and stoles. It is usually left in its natural golden color, with woven motifs in contrasting threads. Muga is sometimes combined with pat or eri silk in the same garment. Small quantities go into ties, handbags and export accessories. Its stiffness and weight suit structured drape rather than soft, fluid garments.
muga-silk.quality: Genuine muga has a natural golden luster that deepens with age and washing, a firm, crisp hand and a relatively high price. Uniform bright gold at a low price suggests dyed mulberry silk, polyester or a blend; adulteration has damaged muga's reputation, according to Assamese reporting. Look for the GI logo, Silk Mark labeling and the seller's authorized-user status, and ask for a test certificate on high-value garments. The Sualkuchi silk testing laboratory and other certified labs test for muga content. Hand-reeled muga shows slight variations in thickness, while perfectly even yarn deserves scrutiny.
pros: The natural golden color needs no dyeing.
Muga is strong and durable, and garments are commonly kept for generations.
A registered geographical indication and GI logo help protect origin.
Outdoor rearing on host trees supports rural Assamese households.
cons: Supply is very small and restricted to one region, so prices are high.
Adulteration and imitation are widespread in the market.
The firm hand is less soft and fluid than mulberry silk.
Production is vulnerable to pollution, weather and disease affecting outdoor rearing.
muga-silk.impact: Muga rearing is an outdoor activity on som and other host trees, needing no irrigation or mulberry cultivation, but it exposes larvae to birds, insects, disease and weather, and research has linked air pollution near industrial sites to stress on host trees. Production is tiny, about 0.6 percent of India's raw silk, so the industry's footprint is small in absolute terms; no life cycle assessment of muga fabric was found. Reeling kills pupae, as with most reeled silk. Socially, muga sustains rearers, reelers and handloom weavers in Assam, and adulteration undercuts genuine producers, which is why the GI logo and testing projects at the Central Muga Eri Research and Training Institute matter.
muga-silk.care: Many Assamese owners hand wash muga in cool water with a mild, neutral soap or shampoo, which traditional accounts say brightens its luster; dry cleaning is an alternative for garments with mixed fibers or zari work. Do not soak for long, wring or scrub. Rinse, roll in a towel and dry in shade, as direct sun can weaken the silk. Iron on the reverse at a low silk setting while slightly damp. Store folded in soft cotton cloth, refolding occasionally to avoid crease breaks, with protection against carpet beetles and silverfish. Keep perfume and deodorant off the fabric. The product label governs.
faq: The color is natural to the silk produced by Antheraea assamensis and is not dyed. It varies slightly with rearing season and host tree, and is often described as deepening with age.
How can I tell real muga from fake?

Buy from authorized GI users, look for the muga GI logo and Silk Mark label, and request a laboratory test for expensive pieces. Real muga has a natural, not glaring, gold and a firm hand; unusually low prices are a warning sign.
Why is muga silk so expensive?

It is produced only in Assam in small quantities, about 230 tonnes a year according to the Ministry of Textiles, by outdoor rearing that is exposed to weather and disease, and it is mainly hand-reeled and handwoven.
Yes. Hand washing in cool water with a mild soap is traditional for muga, and it is known for tolerating washing well. Dry clean pieces with metallic zari or mixed fibers.
notable: Muga Silk of Assam received geographical indication status in 2007 and a registered GI logo in 2014.
Muga makes up well under 1 percent of India's raw silk output.
The Central Muga Eri Research and Training Institute has listed a project to develop a portable analyzer for muga purity in dyed fabrics.
